resources.string: How the obliques turn the trunk

Viewed from above with the front at the top; left and right are the person\'s own sides. Rib cage and pelvis are shown together, with the oblique layers opened up. The pelvis stays still. Muscle emphasis is illustrative and varies with the task.
A fixed pelvis, two muscle layers
The external obliques form the outer layer and the internal obliques lie beneath them. The rib cage can begin to turn over the pelvis without the hips turning with it.
The left external oblique and right internal oblique help turn the rib cage toward the person\'s right. They act from opposite sides of the abdominal wall.
The chest turns back over the same pelvis. As it approaches neutral, the emphasis on the right-turning pair fades; other trunk muscles can help control the motion.
The pairing reverses. The right external oblique and left internal oblique help turn the rib cage toward the person\'s left, with the pelvis still in place.
The rib cage returns to face forward. The left-turning pair is no longer emphasized. Throughout the cycle, the movement is rotation relative to the pelvis.
Abdominal wall from the front: external oblique on the body\'s right, internal oblique exposed on the body\'s left
The outer layer runs mostly down and inward from the side of the rib cage toward the front midline and iliac crest.
Most fibers in this exposed part run up and inward from the iliac crest toward the lower ribs and front midline.
The external oblique starts on the lower eight ribs. The upper fibers of the internal oblique attach to the lowest ribs.
The upper rim of the hip bone anchors fibers from both oblique layers.
The broad tendons of both oblique layers blend toward this fibrous seam at the front midline.
